# The British Miners and the Coal Industry between the Wars 

The problems of the interwar mining industry, which led to a General Strike in 1926, writes W.H. Chaloner, epitomized the struggle between capital and labour in twentieth-century Britain.

 W.H. Chaloner | Published in History Today Volume 14 Issue 6 June 1964 

Between the sixteenth and the nineteenth centuries an expanding coal industry was one of the main factors in Britain’s gradual rise to world economic predominance. The rapid decline between the two World Wars in this hitherto highly successful industry was therefore rendered all the more dramatic and depressing, for a great national enterprise seemed to be surely foundering.

Naturally, much has been written on this subject, but some of the most important evidence from the angle of labour relations has only recently been made available, and this justifies a re-examination of the coal industry’s fate in the 1920s and 1930s.

In 1913 the British coal industry stood at the zenith of its productive success, with a record output of 287 million tons, 94 million tons of which were exported, either for consumption on land or for use in coal-fired shipping. The rise in production had been particularly rapid in the nineteenth century, which saw a twenty-fold increase in output.

The achievements of British coal-owners, engineers and miners generated a climate of optimism, so that those connected with the industry had little doubt in 1919 that the industry’s future would be a successful and profitable one. This illusion was not completely dispelled until 1924-26, for it should be remembered that in 1923 British coal exports, at 104.5 million tons, surpassed the high level of 1913, and total production was only slightly less than in 1913.

The year 1923, however, proved to be an exceptional one, as the great activity in British coal mining resulted partly from the fall in German production caused by the French occupation of the Ruhr and partly from the long strike of the coal miners in the United States of America, both of which events caused a quite fortuitous demand for British coal exports.

Between about 1900 and 1925, and for various reasons, productivity had been at first stagnant and later declining, and the rising output had been secured by a sharp increase in the labour force employed.

Within a year of the outbreak of war in 1914, a quarter of a million miners had enlisted as volunteers in the armed forces, where their skills proved particularly useful in trench warfare. During the war, the record output of 1913 could not be repeated, but the decreased demand for export coal meant that the loss of manpower was not too severely felt.

For example, it has been calculated that the probable loss of output for the first twelve months of the war was 36 million tons, but owing to the loss of export markets the net shortage was only 12 million tons. 1 

As the war progressed, it proved comparatively easy to recruit additional labour from two sources: young men and boys not yet eligible for military service and from the agricultural population. No formal system of apprenticeship existed in coal-mining, except in the case of a minority of auxiliary craftsmen such as carpenters and engineers.

The ranks of the miners had always, up to the 1920’s, been extensively recruited from the agricultural population, particularly as mining wages tended to be about 50 per cent higher than the wages paid to agricultural labourers. Indeed, the records of the miners’ trade unions contain numerous protests against the dilution of the labour force by the influx from the decaying “industry” of farming.

Between 1911 and 1920 the number of those employed in the industry rose from just over one million to just under one million and a quarter. Miners tended to have larger families than the average, and it has been calculated that in the 1920’s between four and five million persons, or between 10 and 12½ per cent of the total population of the United Kingdom, were directly dependent on the coal mines for a livelihood.

The miners themselves were often, but not always, grouped in rural or semi-rural districts, in which the companies responsible for opening up the mines had perforce to provide houses and services for their workers.

Since the economic life of a mine could not be accurately foretold, and since these new settlements were generally remote from urban public utilities, colliery housing tended to be inferior to the general run of working-class housing in construction, standards of accommodation and in sanitary arrangements, although some improvement in these respects can be traced in the later nineteenth century, and “model” mining villages were built by colliery undertakings at Bolsover and Creswell in Derbyshire, for example. 2 

It is a curious anomaly that in the very areas where coal was cheaper than anywhere else in the world, namely, around the British mines, the miners’ cottages usually lacked running hot water. The provision of pithead baths was by no means universal even in 1939-12,000 houses, just over 10,000 of them in England and Wales. 3 

Of these houses 6,460 were built in the expanding coalfields of South Yorkshire, Derbyshire and Nottingham. The cost of such housing varied considerably from enterprise to enterprise, but appears in the 1920’s to have been rarely less than one-third and sometimes nearly half the capital cost of equipping a large new colliery.

The social effects of the miners’ isolation were well expressed in a document issued by the Miners’ Eight Hours’ Day Committee in 1907:

> “A greater degree of solidarity exists in the class of workers in coal mines, taken as a whole, than appears to exist among those engaged in other industries... This sense of solidarity is perhaps largely due to the segregation of the mining population in colliery villages, and their comparative isolation from men engaged in other pursuits, to which must be added the circumstance that they all share together in the sum of the actual employment available, a deficiency of trade causing a universal short week’s working and not a dismissal of individual men.” 4 

The dangerous nature of the underground worker’s task needs little stressing: in 1910, 1,818 miners had been killed at their work, and in 1913 occurred the disaster at Senghenydd pit in South Wales in which no less than 439 miners lost their lives. The enquiry that followed this appalling accident revealed that numerous infractions of the new Coal Mines Act of 1911 had taken place.

The number of miners injured every year always totalled more than 100,000, and the incidence both of deaths and accidents was not appreciably lowered in the early twentieth century. 5 The emotional connection between the high rate of deaths, accidents and disease, on the one hand, and the worker’s demand for the nationalization on the other, is well expressed in the concluding words of B. L. Coombes’s novel of mining life, Those Clouded Hills (1944)—Coombes was an examiner:

> “There is blood on the coal, there will always be blood on the coal, but we feel that blood should be shed for the massfes] who are our kin, not for the enrichment of a few who have battened on our pain in the past.”

It has been said that mining life made the miners the “best trade unionists and the worst politicians” in the United Kingdom. The miners’ leaders of this period had started work in the pits as children at between ten and twelve years of age. Largely self-educated—often as Nonconformist lay preachers—they grew to meet Cabinet Ministers as equals.

They fought Governments, coal-owners and the powerful right-wing section of their own trade-union movement. Given their religious background, the oratory of the pulpit and the imagery of the Bible came naturally to their lips.

In one famous speech of 1921 Frank Hodges, Secretary of the Miners’ Federation, with no blasphemous intent, drew a parallel between his sufferings in the cause of the miners and those of Christ on the cross, 6 while A. J. Cook, his successor as Secretary, referred to the right-wing J. H. Thomas, the General Secretary of the National Union of Railwaymen, as “Judas Iscariot.”

The unyielding stubbornness characteristic of the miner was shared by the owners of the pits. Lord Chancellor Birkenhead, with the epigrammatic exaggeration for which he was famous, stated in the 1920’s: “It would be possible to say without exaggeration of the miners’ leaders that they were the stupidest men in England if we had not frequent occasion to meet the owners.” 7 

And even Neville Chamberlain, no friend of the miners, had to admit that the mine-owners were “not a prepossessing crew.” 8 The ownership of the mines was widely dispersed, and the marketing sector of the industry remained in the 1920’s one of the most highly competitive trades in the United Kingdom. In 1924 there were 2,481 coal mines in the ownership of about 1,400 companies. But, of these, 323 major companies produced 84 per cent of the coal.

Although there were some very large colliery companies, the “typical” concern was one that owned two or three pits only. The mine-owners had organized themselves in county or district associations which at first negotiated directly with the miners’ parallel organizations.

The coal-owners’ organizations were federated nationally into the Mining Association of Great Britain. Originally founded in 1854, the Mining Association had a relatively placid existence up to 1914. It spoke and negotiated for the owners on mining legislation, proposed or in force; but between 1914 and 1946 its powers and influence expanded greatly. 9 

The need for district amalgamations and the closing of the smaller and less efficient pits was recognized by some of the more progressive and ruthless owners, for instance, Sir Charles Markham and Sir Alfred Mond (Lord Melchett). But their proposals, quite naturally, did not prove popular with the smaller companies, particularly when expressed somewhat bluntly, as was the universal custom in the industry.

For example, during the Royal Commission of 1924-25, Sir Charles Markham was asked by the Commissioner, Sir Herbert Samuel, whether he was aware that two-thirds of the mines employed less than 500 men in each and produced only 18 per cent of the total amount of coal raised. Markham, a noted Midlands coal-owner and a sinker of large, deep pits, replied: “That is so. They want shutting up... Today a colliery is no good at all unless it raises 20,000 tons a week. That is about the minimum at which you can begin to expect a colliery to pay.” 10 

By 1943-44 the number of colliery undertakings had fallen to 750, controlling 1,588 mines, as the result of amalgamations after 1926 and the closing of many uneconomic mines in the 1930’s. 11 

By the end of the nineteenth century the miners had built up a powerful trade-union structure, based on county organizations, which were loosely united from 1888 onwards in the Miners’ Federation of Great Britain.

The county or district organizations which formed the Federation sometimes had little love for one another, and internal disputes were frequent. The Federation has been replaced since January 1st, 1945, by the more centralized National Union of Mineworkers, and the county organizations have lost much of their power.

The Miners’ Federation soon made its mark on national politics. As early as 1894 the fifth Annual Conference of the Federation passed a resolution by a large majority in favour of nationalizing the coal mines, and in 1913 an unsuccessful Bill to nationalize “the coal mines and minerals of the United Kingdom and to provide for the national distribution and sale of coal” had been introduced into the House of Commons by Members from the Labour Party.
